We hosted a 𝗥𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗼𝗻 𝗕𝗶𝗼-𝗔𝗜: 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘆-𝗔𝗰𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗺𝗶𝗮 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻, in collaboration with Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) Hyderabad, the Institute of genomics and integrative biology (CSIR) and the BRIC - Centre for DNA Fingerprinting and Diagnostics (CDFD).

Dr. Satya Prakash Dash, Prof. Ullas Kolthur and Dr. Anand Anandkumar initiated the session. This was followed by speakers from academia, startups and industry sharing their expertise, with the aim of identifying, generating and building real collaborations and partnerships that are problem specific.

The discussion highlighted the need for good-quality datasets that are specific to our population and geography; compute that is still too slow for the work being asked of it; and the design-build-test-learn cycle — keeping the lab inside the loop, so that every computational prediction meets an experiment and every experimental result improves the next model. Alongside this came the harder question of validation, and what metrics we should be using to build and judge these algorithms in the first place.

The emphasis was on building shared, open capability rather than parallel private efforts.

Our thanks to every speaker and participant for their time and open conversation.

🔹 𝐒𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 8: From Patent Grant to Enforcement: Identifying Infringement and Protecting MedTech Innovations
👤 𝐒𝐩𝐞𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐫 : 𝐌𝐫. 𝐍𝐚𝐯𝐞𝐞𝐧 𝐌𝐚𝐭𝐡𝐮𝐫
Senior Patent Expert | Former Joint Controller of Patents & Designs, Indian Patent Office, Ministry of Commerce & Industry, Government of India

The session will provide researchers, faculty members, inventors, and technology innovators with practical insights into patent infringement and post-grant patent protection. Participants will learn how to analyse granted patent claims, identify potential infringement by competing products or technologies, evaluate technical evidence, and understand the difference between Patent Infringement Analysis and Freedom-to-Operate (FTO) Analysis. Through practical MedTech examples involving medical devices, AI, software, and diagnostic technologies, the session will also cover market monitoring, evidence preservation, claim mapping, and the commercial and legal considerations involved in protecting innovations after patent grant. 

🔹 𝐒𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 9:
Beyond Patent Filing: An Inventor’s Role in Patent Prosecution, FER Responses and Hearings
👤 𝐒𝐩𝐞𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐫 : 𝐌𝐬. 𝐌𝐨𝐧𝐢𝐤𝐚
Intellectual Property Professional

The session will provide researchers, inventors, faculty members, and technology innovators with practical insights into their role during patent prosecution, from examination to grant. Participants will learn how to review First Examination Reports (FERs), understand novelty and inventive-step objections, analyse cited prior art, identify distinguishing technical features, and effectively communicate technical differences and their effects. The session will also cover evaluating proposed claim amendments, assessing their necessity and impact on patent scope, and supporting patent professionals during patent hearings. Through practical examples and prior-art comparison exercises, the session aims to help inventors become active technical contributors throughout the patent prosecution process. 

📅 Session Date: 15 October 2026

 📍 Venue: IIT Mandi Catalyst, IIT Mandi, Kamand Campus, Himachal Pradesh – 175005, India

🚀 Building Stronger Sales Foundations for Startup Growth

IIT Mandi Catalyst recently hosted an insightful workshop on 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐠𝐲 & 𝐄𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐂𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐫 𝐀𝐜𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧, featuring practical perspectives on enterprise sales principles and founder-led customer acquisition focused on delivering measurable business outcomes.

The session was led by Mr. Sandeep Bhatnagar, Co-founder & Board Member, Xloud Technologies, who shared valuable insights on developing effective sales strategies and acquiring early customers. Ask someone to define a social enterprise, and you will hear a familiar answer. Low profits. Services for the poor. A business with its heart in the right place... 

Then push a little:

Does a low-cost TB vaccine qualify? A device that allows home screening for cervical cancer in rural households? Affordable diagnostic devices? A household-level biodigester? Sodium-ion batteries for energy storage? Green concrete? Soil-microbiome restoration? Effluent treatment that returns clean water to the planet? 

The reflex comes quickly. "That is deep science, not social." 

That reflex is the myth. The deeper error is treating "science" and "social" as competing categories. They answer different questions. Science describes the risk you are taking. Social describes whose problem you have chosen, and whether the market can capture the return. 

So what should earn the word social? Not the legal structure. Not the optics. Not whether the founder has chosen to make a profit. Two questions do the work:

1 - What problem are you solving that the market is not already solving?
2- What risk are you absorbing that conventional enterprise refuses to hold? 

Seen this way, a deep-science venture addressing a neglected disease, climate resilience, clean energy, water security or sustainable materials is every bit as much an act of social entrepreneurship as a last-mile service-delivery organisation. 

The misclassification has consequences. The problem is not semantic. We have built capital systems around categories, and an innovation that does not fit the category becomes orphaned. It is why some of the most consequential technologies society needs struggle to get funded, and why some never get built.

For decades, our most celebrated social enterprises created new models to reach people conventional markets had overlooked. Amul, Aravind Eye Care, SELCO and many others redesigned distribution, financing, access and delivery. That work remains essential.

But the frontier is moving upstream. The hardest problems we now face cannot be solved through distribution innovation alone. Sometimes the missing molecule, material, diagnostic, energy system or production technology simply does not exist. It has to be invented. And once invented, it still has to be tested, validated, financed, deployed, adopted and taken to scale. Which means the social entrepreneur of the future is as likely to emerge from a laboratory, an engineering workshop or a clinical validation site as from a development organisation.

The defining question was never profit versus non-profit. It is whether you are solving problems society urgently needs solved and markets systematically undervalue, and whether you will take the scientific, entrepreneurial and market-creation risks required to solve them. Increasingly, those problems run through deep science. That is not outside social entrepreneurship. It is its next frontier.
#SocialEntrepreneurship #DeepTech #DeepScience #innovation Social Alpha

Phool asked a question nobody else had asked: what can we do with flower waste?

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐒𝐜𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞. The first answer was flowercycling, turning temple flowers into incense. A good answer, and a tempting place to stop. Phool kept asking. That persistence turned a flower-recycling company into a biomaterials company. Fleather was only the start. You don't build new materials by rebranding old ones. You build them in the lab, one experiment at a time.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐄𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐞𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐮𝐫𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩. Science on its own doesn't reach the market. Someone has to take the risk nobody else will underwrite, translate science into products, find customers for a material that didn't exist, and survive the long gap between proof of concept and a working business. Most good ideas die in that gap. This one didn't.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐈𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐜𝐭. None of it began with a technology. It began with empathy for a polluted river and for the women whose livelihoods now depend on this work. That empathy never became a side project. As the science deepened, the impact widened: social, economic and environmental.
Phool grew on all three at once. This is science and society converging, driven by entrepreneurial risk-taking. #skininthegame

From Lab Bench to Livestock Economy: Conversations with an Investor

As part of the City Camp at TANUVAS, participants had the opportunity to engage in a special session on “Conversations with an Investor”, led by Gowtham Sarvesh R R, Partner & Chief Operating Officer, Keiretsu Forum Chennai & Singapore.

The session offered an investor’s perspective on the opportunities and challenges facing science-led ventures in animal health, feed, nutrition, veterinary sciences and food technology.

Key discussions focused on:
🔹 Where capital is looking and the opportunities for science-led ventures
🔹 What investors look for beyond good science—market validation, paying customers, evidence and unit economics
🔹 Bridging the gap between research and investor readiness
🔹 Turning real-world problems into opportunities worth building solutions for
🔹 How founders can communicate their problem, customer, evidence and commercial milestones more effectively to investors

The session encouraged participants to look at their research and innovations through a new lens—not just “Is this a good idea?”, but also “Who needs it, what problem does it solve, and what evidence will make it investable?”

A big thank you to Gowtham Sarvesh for sharing valuable insights and perspectives with our participants!
